knownFor: Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour
Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences (1979)
legacy: Sir Arthur Lewis is regarded as one of the founders of development economics and one of the most influential economists of the twentieth century. His theories transformed how economists understand economic growth in developing nations, particularly the transition from agricultural economies to industrial economies. His work continues to guide policymakers, researchers, and international organizations concerned with poverty reduction, industrialization, and economic development.
earlyLife: William Arthur Lewis was born on 23 January 1915 in Castries, Saint Lucia. Demonstrating exceptional academic ability from an early age, he advanced rapidly through school and earned a scholarship to the London School of Economics. There he studied economics and became one of the first people of African-Caribbean heritage to achieve distinction in the British academic world.
scientificField: Lewis worked primarily in economics, development economics, labor economics, economic growth theory, international development, and public policy. His research focused on understanding how poor nations can achieve sustainable economic growth and improve living standards.
majorContributions: Lewis's most famous contribution was the Lewis Model, also known as the Dual-Sector Model. He argued that economic development can occur when surplus labor moves from low-productivity agricultural sectors into higher-productivity industrial sectors. His landmark paper 'Economic Development with Unlimited Supplies of Labour' became one of the foundational works of development economics. Lewis also contributed extensively to studies of wages, industrialization, trade, capital formation, and economic planning in developing countries.
laterLife: Lewis held prominent academic positions at institutions including the University of Manchester, Princeton University, and the University of the West Indies. In 1963 he became the first Vice-Chancellor of the University of the West Indies. His contributions gained worldwide recognition, and in 1979 he received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his pioneering research on economic development and structural change.
whyImportant: Arthur Lewis provided economists and policymakers with powerful tools for understanding how nations develop economically. His ideas influenced development strategies across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. Much of modern development economics, including discussions about industrialization, labor migration, productivity, and poverty reduction, continues to build upon the foundations established by Lewis.
